table.brief: Link inventory: Page title / URL (long unbreakable URLs) / Last checked / Status code

understanding.purpose: Audit a set of links by identifying each page and URL alongside its most recent check and resulting status code.
understanding.reading: Readers scan page titles to find an entry, follow the row to its URL, and compare check dates and status codes across entries. Wrapped titles and URLs can share the same row height, provided each row remains easy to follow.
groups: Page title and URL identify the same destination; the title supports scanning while the URL gives the precise address.
Last checked and Status code describe the result of the audit and should remain compact and easy to compare vertically.
keep_intact: Individual words in page titles and column headers
may_wrap: Page titles at natural word boundaries

preferred.name: r1A
preferred.note: Move 25px from the URL to the title relative to r0A. This tests whether titles can wrap more naturally while preserving substantially more URL space than r0B.

preferred.name: r3C
preferred.note: Test a modest shift from the URL to the title column, preserving nearly all of r2A's address width while seeking a better title wrap.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Test a middle ground closer to r0B: give titles more room than the balanced option while restoring 15px to URLs compared with r0B.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Move 10px from the title to the URL column to test whether addresses wrap more naturally while titles remain easy to scan.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Test a middle ground between r1A and r1B, giving URLs another 20px over r1A while retaining more title space than r1B.

acceptable.name: r3A
acceptable.note: Give the title column 15px more than r2A to test whether the deprecated API title can read more compactly, while retaining substantial URL space and intact audit headers.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Try a stronger allocation to page titles, which are the primary scanning entry point. The URL column remains wider than the longest unbreakable URL segment, though addresses may wrap more.

bad.name: r1B
bad.note: Give URLs 15px more than r0A to test whether domain and path breaks improve. The title column still accommodates its longest word, though more title wrapping is likely.
bad.why: The narrow title column fragments several page titles into three or four lines, making the primary labels harder to scan and creating uneven, tall rows. The extra URL width does not compensate for that loss.

rationale: r1A and r3C give page titles enough room to remain readily scannable while leaving the largest share for URLs. Both keep headers and dates on one line, avoid mid-word splits, and retain a consistent row rhythm. The small difference in title and URL widths does not produce a meaningful visual advantage for either design.

general: Give identifying labels enough width to support scanning, even when another column contains longer strings.
Allocate width according to content and reading task; compact fields need less space than narrative text or identifiers.
Judge line breaks and row rhythm together, rather than treating minimum table height as the sole goal.
specific: The URL column needs the largest share, while the date and status columns fit their headers at 105px and 97px.
A title width around 180–185px balances title legibility with URL wrapping in the rendered candidates.

tradeoffs: Wider titles make some labels more comfortable to read, while wider URLs can preserve longer stretches of address on each line. The preferred pair balances those needs without an extra line in the careers row.
uncertain: The ranges are conservative estimates based on the rendered candidates, not tested breakpoints; intermediate widths and changes to the two compact columns may also work. A designer prioritizing longer title phrases could reasonably prefer r1C or r3B.

critique.good: The generous URL column keeps addresses to two or three lines, and the compact audit columns make dates and status codes easy to compare. Rows remain clearly separated.
critique.problems: Page titles are harder to scan because every title wraps, and two extend to three lines. Several URLs also break within the hyphenated domain, making the address harder to follow.
critique.cause: The 160px title column leaves only 139px for text. Even the 404px URL column cannot keep every long address or hyphenated domain together at the available break points.

critique.good: Titles have a more comfortable measure, mostly occupying one or two lines. The audit columns retain clear, single-line headers and values.
critique.problems: Several URLs take three lines and break within domains or path components, leaving tall rows with unused space beneath shorter titles and audit values.
critique.cause: Moving 60px from the URL to the title reduces the URL text area to 323px. This improves title wrapping but makes more addresses determine the row height.

critique.good: The wider title column makes several page names easy to scan, and dates and status codes remain aligned and intact.
critique.problems: The first two addresses extend to four lines, producing especially tall rows and large empty areas in the other columns. Frequent URL breaks make the precise addresses harder to trace.
critique.cause: The 253px title column leaves only 311px for URLs, or 290px of text space, just above the reported longest unbreakable segment.

critique.good: The title column keeps every title to one or two lines, making entries easy to scan. Dates and codes form compact, consistent columns, and all headers remain on one line. The two- and three-line URLs fit comfortably within their rows.
critique.problems: Several addresses break inside the hyphenated domain, so readers must reassemble the host across lines. The longest URLs still occupy three lines, creating tall rows beside shorter titles.
critique.cause: The 379px URL column cannot accommodate some longer address segments alongside preceding text; the 185px title column uses space that might help the URLs, although reducing it too far harms title scanning.

critique.good: The wider URL column keeps the first address to two lines and gives addresses more horizontal room. Dates, codes, and headers remain intact and aligned.
critique.problems: Titles become ragged and difficult to scan: the Salesforce title occupies four lines, and several others occupy three. These wraps make multiple rows taller even when the adjacent URL needs fewer lines.
critique.cause: At 145px, the title column provides only 124px for text. Giving those 40px to the URL column saves some URL wrapping but causes more disruptive title wrapping.

critique.good: The wider title column gives titles a relaxed measure and keeps them to at most two lines. Audit results remain compact and easy to compare.
critique.problems: The careers URL takes three lines, leaving extra vertical space beside its one-line title. Other long addresses remain heavily wrapped, and domains still split across lines.
critique.cause: The 205px title column takes 20px from the URL compared with r1A; the resulting 359px URL column forces an additional line in the careers row without reducing the maximum number of title lines.

critique.good: The title column supports scanning, and the Salesforce title stays on two lines. Dates, status codes, and all headers remain intact and align consistently. Horizontal rules keep the wrapped content together as rows.
critique.problems: The deprecated API title takes three lines, while several URL lines end with short fragments. The first and last URLs also leave a single word or short phrase on their third line.
critique.cause: The 175px title column forces the API title onto a third line. The 389px URL column breaks long addresses at available punctuation, sometimes leaving short final lines.

critique.good: Dates, status codes, and headers remain intact, and the rows are easy to follow. The 399px URL column gives addresses slightly more room without increasing the table height.
critique.problems: The Salesforce title now takes three lines, making the identifying column more fragmented. The added URL width does not reduce any row height, and several addresses still have short final lines.
critique.cause: Reducing the title column to 165px forces the Salesforce title onto a third line. Increasing the URL column to 399px does not cross a useful wrapping threshold for these rows.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r2A.why: The URL has useful room, and dates and status codes stay intact. Several titles wrap to two or three lines, including a three-line legacy title.

ref_equal.why: The narrow URL column breaks addresses across many lines and even splits words, while the date and status columns have excessive empty space.

ref_auto.why: The wide URL column helps addresses, but every date splits across two lines and both right-hand headers wrap, making the audit fields harder to scan.

r1B.why: Dates and status codes remain intact and URLs have room, but the narrow title column forces several titles into three or four lines.

r1C.why: Titles are easy to scan and dates and codes stay intact. The narrower URL column makes some addresses wrap to three lines, including the careers URL.

r1A.why: Titles and URLs share the available space well: titles take at most two lines, URLs mostly take two or three, and dates and status codes remain intact.

raw.unsure: A and E are also strong; the preference between them depends on how much priority readers give URL continuity versus scanning page titles.

r1C.why: Titles generally fit in one or two lines, and dates and codes remain intact. Several URLs wrap across three lines, often splitting the domain, but rows remain easy to scan.

r1A.why: Balances readable two-line titles with a generous URL column. Dates, codes and headers stay intact, and the rows have a consistent, compact rhythm.

ref_equal.why: The narrow URL column breaks addresses into many fragments, while the date and status columns contain large expanses of unused space. Tall rows make the audit harder to scan.

ref_auto.why: The wide URL column comes at the cost of narrow titles and dates: every date breaks across lines, and both right-hand headers wrap. This makes comparisons less immediate.

r1B.why: URLs have ample room and dates stay intact, but the title column is cramped: several titles take three or four lines, making page identification slower.

r2A.why: URLs have room and dates and codes remain intact. The narrower title column creates several three-line titles, giving it a less even reading rhythm than B.

raw.unsure: A and B are close; the preferred balance depends partly on whether readers prioritize scanning page titles or following URL text.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
